clinical_knowledge.topic: Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria evaluation and management
core_concepts: Chronic spontaneous urticaria is defined as recurrent hives (with or without angioedema) occurring almost daily for six weeks or more without an identifiable external trigger.
Individual wheals are transient, typically resolving within 24 hours, but new lesions continually appear elsewhere on the body.
Unlike acute urticaria, an external allergic trigger is rarely found; broad food or environmental allergy testing is usually unnecessary.
First-line treatment is scheduled (not as-needed) second-generation H1-antihistamines, up-titrated to up to four times the standard dose before considering omalizumab.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent itchy red welts on skin lasting less than 24 hours for 2 months

Key HPI features: 23F reports 2 months of daily, intensely itchy, raised red skin plaques (hives) that appear suddenly on various body parts. Each individual welt fades completely within 12-18 hours, but new ones appear constantly. No throat swelling.
Objective/Exam findings: Transient, blanching, erythematous wheals may be seen if examined during an active flare; none present between episodes. No angioedema.
common_misconceptions: Ordering extensive food or environmental allergy panels, which are rarely helpful since chronic spontaneous urticaria is not usually triggered by a specific allergen.
Treating antihistamines only as needed (PRN) rather than on a scheduled basis, which under-treats the daily symptom burden.
Assuming the condition is dangerous or airway-threatening when there is no angioedema or throat involvement.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to allergic contact dermatitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Individual welts lasting more than 24 hours or bruising.
management_principles: Explain that a specific external trigger is rarely identified in chronic spontaneous urticaria, unlike acute urticaria.
Start a scheduled (not PRN) second-generation antihistamine (e.g., fexofenadine or cetirizine), up-titrating to up to 4x standard dose if needed.
Consider omalizumab for antihistamine-refractory disease after specialist evaluation.
Refer to Allergy/Immunology if symptoms persist despite an adequate antihistamine trial.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Itchy hives appearing almost daily for six weeks or more, each welt fading within 24 hours, usually without an identifiable trigger.
red_flags: Individual welts lasting more than 24 hours or bruising

must_ask.say: How many weeks has this been happening?
Does each welt go away within a day?
Has your throat ever swollen or felt tight?
Have you noticed anything that seems to bring on new hives — a food, detergent, stress?
Have you had any allergy testing done for this?
